prompt: Which statements describe marketing insights?

options.text: Knowledge and understanding about a market, its consumers and the companies operating within it
They are generated through observation of consumer, company and stakeholder behaviour
They are fundamental to understand a marketplace and identify emerging trends
Marketing insights and marketing research are the same thing

explanation: Marketing research ≠ marketing insights: research is one of the tools for discovery, insights are the deeper understanding that results.

prompt: Which are the three key moments for marketing insights?

options.text: Looking back – past behaviour and historical market data
Focus on the present – tracking behaviour in real time (e.g. Voice of Customer, NPS)
Looking forward – predicting behaviour through trend forecasting and statistical modelling

explanation: Looking back, real time and looking forward.

basis.ref: Seite 7 – Key Moments for Marketing Insights

prompt: Primary research methods …

options.text: … involve data already collected for other purposes

explanation: Primary data are collected for a specific purpose and can be experimental/non-experimental and qualitative/quantitative. Data collected for other purposes and internal/external sources describe secondary research. Past exam question.

prompt: Which statements about secondary research are correct?

options.text: It uses data that have already been compiled
It can draw on internal and external sources
It is usually more time- and cost-effective than primary research
It is always collected for the specific purpose of the current study

explanation: Data collected for a specific purpose = primary research.

prompt: Which are key sections of a market analysis based on secondary data?
explanation: A market analysis assesses market size (volume and value), segments, competition, channels, barriers to entry and regulation (incl. compliance costs).

prompt: Which database is described as "an insights platform that documents new consumer behaviour and key industry trends across different consumer markets"?
explanation: Euromonitor: international market analyses, consumer/country/company data. Statista: international statistics portal. Xerfi: industry studies on French and international markets.

prompt: Which elements should be used to structure a trend in order to analyse it adequately?

options.text: Basic needs, drivers of change and innovations

explanation: The fundamental trend elements are basic needs, drivers of change and innovations (Mason et al., 2015). Maturity, industry and locality are used to EVALUATE a trend for opportunity. Past exam question.

prompt: Which criteria are used to evaluate a trend for opportunity (Mattin et al., 2015)?
explanation: How are the expectations behind the trend playing out now (maturity), in my target locality, and in my industry?

basis.ref: Seite 31 – Choosing which trend to apply

prompt: Which statements on macro and micro trends are correct?

options.text: A macro trend spans at least five years and impacts a variety of industries
A micro trend moves from early influencers to mass adoption within one to two years
Micro trends tend to be smaller-scale realisations of desires underlying macro trends
The wellness boom is an example of a micro trend

explanation: The maker movement and the wellness boom are examples of macro trends.

prompt: Which techniques do trend forecasters use to detect emerging trends?
explanation: Weak signals (anomalies, meaningful in clusters), cultural brailling (Faith Popcorn: sensing change daily), horizon scanning (structured scanning of the STEEPLE landscape).

prompt: Which belong to the ANALYSE section of the Consumer Trend Canvas?
explanation: Innovation potential and "Who" belong to the APPLY section.

basis.ref: Seite 33 – A tool for generating trend-driven

prompt: In the Consumer Trend Canvas, how do shifts and triggers differ?

options.text: Shifts are long-term macro changes playing out over years or decades
Triggers are more immediate changes, e.g. new technologies, political events, economic shocks
An aging society or urban transition are typical triggers
Shifts and triggers together form the drivers of change

explanation: Aging society, rich–poor divide, climate challenge, people on the move, urban transition and emerging middle class are SHIFTS.

prompt: Where can a trend be applied according to the "Innovation potential" box of the canvas?
explanation: Vision (long-term), business model (new venture/brand), product/service/experience, marketing & communication.

prompt: What are the drivers of change fuelling this trend? (select all that apply)
explanation: The text names the climate challenge (shift), the cost-of-living crisis after the 2022 energy shock (trigger) and AI-powered resale apps (technology trigger). Aging is not mentioned – stick to the text.

basis.ref: im Stil von Mock exam 2025/26, Exercise 3 (Trendanalyse)

prompt: What new consumer expectations are created by this trend? (select all that apply)

options.text: Brands take responsibility for a product's second life (take-back, certified resale, repair)
Reselling is as easy as posting a story
Lower prices for new fast-fashion items

explanation: The text describes expectations of take-back, certified resale and repair, and effortless reselling. Cheaper fast fashion or faster delivery are not supported by the text.

basis.ref: im Stil von Mock exam 2025/26, Exercise 3 (Trendanalyse)

prompt: Which basic needs does this trend satisfy? (select all that apply)

options.text: Status / self-expression (badge of taste, standing out)

explanation: A rare vintage piece is a badge of taste (status, self-expression); keeping up with fashion more cheaply addresses financial security. The other options are not in the text.

basis.ref: im Stil von Mock exam 2025/26, Exercise 3 (Trendanalyse)

statement: A consumer trend is a new manifestation among people – in behaviour, attitude or expectation – of a fundamental human need, want or desire.
explanation: Definition by Mason et al. (2015).

statement: Innovations are trends.
explanation: Innovations are not trends but examples of how a trend exists. On-trend innovations cater to needs while anticipating or responding to change.

statement: Basic human needs change frequently, which is why trends emerge.
explanation: Basic needs are fundamental and rarely-if-ever-changing; what changes are the drivers of change and the ways needs are served.

statement: There are no trends without change.
explanation: Analysing change (drivers of change) is at the core of trend forecasting.

statement: Trend forecasting combines intuition, hard data and experience.
explanation: The anatomy of a trend: intuition + hard data + experience.

basis.ref: Seite 19 – The Anatomy of a Trend

statement: Horizon scanning is the unstructured, daily sensing of changes through feeling, smelling and tasting.
explanation: That describes cultural brailling (Faith Popcorn). Horizon scanning is a more organised, structured approach to detect shifts in the social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical landscape.

statement: Weak signals become meaningful when they are organised in clusters across industries.
explanation: On their own they are random, disconnected and could be surreal.

statement: Because adoption of new products is fluid, the traditional innovation adoption curve (Rogers, 1962) may be unreliable in today's dynamic contexts.
explanation: That is why trends must be adapted for today (trend maturity).

basis.ref: Seite 31 – Choosing which trend to apply

statement: New consumer expectations are usually set within your own industry.
explanation: New expectations of quality of service are usually set OUTSIDE your industry and affect it later – monitor other industries.

statement: Emerging consumer expectations can be identified by looking for gaps between what consumers want and what they currently have.
explanation: Expectation gaps reveal unmet needs.

statement: A persona is a rich description of one fictional person exemplifying a specific group of people.
explanation: Personas help to create empathy and better ideas in the APPLY section ("Who").

statement: Secondary data is usually more time- and cost-effective than primary data.
explanation: It has already been compiled and is often widely available.

statement: The marketing research process has five steps: problem formulation, sources & research design, data collection method, data collection, data analysis & interpretation.
explanation: Steps 2 and 3 concern the types of data and methods to collect them.

statement: Regulation in a market analysis includes estimating compliance costs.
explanation: Compliance costs are costs a company incurs to adhere to industry- or country-specific regulations.

statement: The rising popularity of resale apps among Gen Z is a basic need.
explanation: It is an innovation/manifestation. The underlying basic needs are e.g. status/self-expression and security.

basis.ref: im Stil von Mock exam 2025/26, Exercise 3 (Trendanalyse)

statement: Based on the text, ageing society is a driver of change of the Generation I trend.
explanation: The trend is driven by digital natives growing up with intuitive technology and by more wealth/spending power – ageing is not mentioned.

statement: According to the text, Generation I members have access to more wealth than previous generations.
explanation: Toys worth £1,200, allowances of $780 a year, influence on $1.12 trillion of family spending.

basis.ref: Zusatzfrage zum Fall aus Klausur 2019/20, Mini case Generation I

prompt: Recalling the Consumer Trend Canvas structure, what are the drivers of change related to the Generation I trend?
modelAnswer: Shifts: digitalisation of everyday life – digital natives born after 2002 grow up with a constant layer of effortless technological augmentation; they no longer notice technology. Triggers: intuitive touch and swipe devices, video calling and creative apps (ATOMS, Flip Boom) that let kids build and share their own worlds instantly. Economic driver: Generation I has access to more wealth (toys worth £1,200, $780 allowance, influence on $1.12 trillion family spending) and rarely saves.
keyPoints: Intuitive touch devices, apps, video calls (triggers)
Shorter cognitive processes, expectation of immediacy
More wealth / spending power and influence on family spending

basis.ref: Mini case Generation I & Playmobil a)

prompt: If you were the brand manager of Playmobil, what factors would you consider to adapt the Generation I trend to your business and how would you leverage it?
modelAnswer: Evaluate the trend for opportunity: trend maturity (how are expectations for intuitive, interactive experiences playing out now?), industry (how are other toy and tech firms serving it?) and locality (which markets?). Then apply it: product/experience – combine physical sets with apps, AR or customisation so kids can create their own worlds; marketing – simple, direct but rich digital communication on the platforms kids use; who – target Gen I as users but also parents as payers, given children's influence on family spending; consider ethics/regulation when marketing to children.
keyPoints: Marketing via digital channels, simple and direct

basis.ref: Mini case Generation I & Playmobil b)

prompt: Explain the two sections of the Consumer Trend Canvas and the boxes they contain.
modelAnswer: ANALYSE (left side) unpacks the trend: inspirations (innovations raising expectations), basic needs (deep needs and desires the trend addresses), drivers of change (shifts = long-term macro changes; triggers = immediate changes such as technologies, events, shocks) and emerging consumer expectations (new needs created by the changes). APPLY (right side) uses these insights: innovation potential (vision, business model, product/service/experience, marketing) and who (which new customer groups, e.g. via personas).
keyPoints: Analyse: inspirations, basic needs, drivers of change, emerging expectations
Drivers of change = shifts and triggers
Apply: innovation potential (vision, business model, product/service/experience, marketing)
Apply: who – target customer groups / personas

prompt: State the key sections of a market analysis.
modelAnswer: Industry description and outlook (size, trends, life cycle, growth); target market (segments, demographics, psychographics, needs, size and value); competitive analysis (positioning, strengths, weaknesses, strategies); distribution channels; barriers to entry; regulation (compliance costs).

statement: Trend identification draws on very diverse sources of inspiration, e.g. geopolitics, local subcultures, influencers, biotechnology and demographic shifts.
explanation: Horizon scanning looks far beyond one's own industry to spot weak signals early.

statement: Uber changing what people expect from transport (instant, one-touch service) is an example of expectation transfer.
explanation: Once experienced, such expectations transfer to other industries – people expect the same convenience from banks, food delivery, healthcare.

statement: Basic needs, drivers of change and innovations are the fundamental elements of a consumer trend.
explanation: Trend = basic needs + drivers of change (shifts, triggers) → innovations → new consumer expectations.

statement: Emerging consumer expectations are tied to a specific geography, industry and market and do not spread across borders.
explanation: Expectations spread across industries (expectation transfer) and countries, especially through digital media.

statement: A new consumer trend emerges when an external change unlocks a new way to serve basic human needs.
explanation: Needs stay stable; change (technology, society, economy) creates new ways to serve them.

statement: Consumer trends are only about fashion and design.
explanation: Trends concern how we live, eat, travel, work, consume media and relate to each other.

statement: Consumer trends are created by trend forecasting agencies such as WGSN, TrendWatching or The Future Laboratory.
explanation: Agencies identify and describe trends; trends emerge from changes in society and consumer behaviour.

statement: Macro trends matter mainly to fashion companies and much less to the mass market.
explanation: Macro trends are broad, long-lasting shifts affecting many industries and mass markets.

statement: Innovations are manifestations of how a trend exists.
explanation: Innovations are evidence of a trend, not the trend itself – the trend is the underlying shift in behaviour or expectations.

statement: Trend forecasting is a method for identifying short-term changes in the retail and service industries.
explanation: It looks at medium- to long-term shifts in consumer needs and expectations across all industries.

statement: Macro trends affect a variety of industries and have a long-lasting effect on consumer behaviour.
explanation: They unfold over many years (e.g. digitalisation, ageing, sustainability) and shape many markets.
